terms.definition: The part of a machine that turns a control signal into action in the physical world, such as a motor, servo, speaker, or LED.
A mixture of two or more metals (or a metal and another element) combined to create a material with properties neither has alone, such as the tin-silver-copper mix used in lead-free solder.
Electric current that reverses direction many times a second, so its voltage keeps flipping polarity. Wall outlets in North America supply AC at 60 Hz.

A meter (or a multimeter's current mode) that measures electric current. It has very low resistance, so it must be placed in series so that the current flows through it, never across a voltage source.
The unit of electric current, written A. One amp is one coulomb of charge passing a point each second. Named after André-Marie Ampère.
The height of a wave: how far it swings from its middle value to its peak. For AC, the amplitude is the peak voltage.
A signal that can take any value in a range, like a voltage that slides smoothly from 0 V to 5 V. An Arduino reads it with analogRead() as a number from 0 to 1023.
A circuit that measures a voltage and turns it into a number; on an Arduino UNO it maps 0–5 V to 0–1023, which analogRead() returns.
The terminal where conventional current enters a diode or LED: the positive side. On a new LED it is the longer leg; on the schematic symbol it is the flat side of the triangle.
A meter feature that picks the measurement range automatically and shows a prefix such as m, k, or M, so you must read the unit letters to know the value's size.
How many signal symbols per second a serial link sends, such as 9600. Both ends must use the same baud rate or the text arrives as gibberish.
A number system with only two digits, 0 and 1. Each binary digit, or bit, can be stored as one LOW or HIGH voltage.
The math of true and false, combined with NOT, AND, and OR, named for George Boole; it describes both logic gates and the && || ! operators in code.
A reusable prototyping board with a grid of push-fit sockets that lets components and jumper wires be connected and rearranged without soldering.
How much charge a capacitor stores for each volt across it, measured in farads (F). Real parts are usually microfarads (µF) or smaller.
A part that stores electric charge on two conducting plates separated by an insulator. It can release that charge quickly, smooth out bumpy voltage, or block DC while passing AC.
The tendency of a liquid to flow into narrow spaces without outside help, which is how solder wick draws up molten solder during desoldering.

The terminal where conventional current leaves a diode or LED: the negative side, marked by the bar on the symbol, the stripe on a diode, and the short leg and flat edge of an LED. In a vacuum tube it is the heated electrode that gives off electrons.
The 0-volt reference point of a circuit, usually the battery’s − side. Every voltage is measured from it, and every current path returns to it.
Every point joined by plain wire, which all share one voltage. On a breadboard, each connected row of five holes is one node.
A steady square wave that tells a digital circuit when to take its next step; an Arduino UNO's clock ticks 16 million times a second (16 MHz).

Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor: chips that pair N-channel and P-channel MOSFETs in every gate so almost no current flows except while switching, which is why modern processors can run on batteries.
A joint where the solder never fully bonded because the metals were too cool, the flux was used up, or the joint moved while hardening. It looks dull, grainy, or lumpy and conducts unreliably.
A material, like copper, whose electrons move easily, so current flows through it with little resistance.
An unbroken electrical path between two points, usually confirmed with a multimeter's continuity or beep test before trusting a joint.
The agreed direction for drawing current: out of the + terminal, through the circuit, and back to −. Electrons actually drift the other way, but every schematic symbol and arrow uses this convention.
The unit of electric charge, written C: the charge of about 6.24 billion billion electrons. One amp is one coulomb per second. Named after Charles-Augustin de Coulomb.
Ignoring the rapid on-off flickers a mechanical switch makes for a few milliseconds when it is pressed, so one press counts as one press.
A small capacitor, usually 100 nF, placed right next to a chip's power pin to supply sudden bursts of current so the supply voltage doesn't dip.
Removing solder from a joint to free a component or correct a mistake, typically with solder wick, a solder sucker, or a hot air station.
The moment an insulator such as air suddenly starts to conduct because the voltage across it is too high, producing a spark. Dry air breaks down at roughly 3 million volts per meter.
A signal with only two states, HIGH or LOW (on or off, 1 or 0), such as a button that is either pressed or not.
A one-way valve for electric current. Current flows from anode to cathode and is blocked the other way, which makes diodes the parts used for rectification and reverse-polarity protection.

A multimeter mode that pushes about 1 mA through a part and displays the voltage across it. It shows a diode's or LED's forward voltage in one direction and OL in the other, revealing which lead is the anode.
Electric current that keeps flowing in one direction, so its voltage keeps one polarity. Batteries, solar cells, USB, and Arduino boards all use DC.
The percentage of each PWM cycle that the signal is on. 25% duty cycle is on a quarter of the time; 100% is always on.
A property of particles that makes them push or pull on each other: like charges repel and opposite charges attract. Electrons are negative, protons positive. Measured in coulombs.
The flow of electric charge past a point each second, measured in amperes (A). Its symbol in equations is I.
A machine that turns electricity into spinning motion using the push between magnets and current-carrying coils. A generator run backward.
A can-shaped capacitor with large capacitance for its size that is polarized: the striped leg must go to the lower voltage, and it must never exceed its voltage rating.
Making a voltage in a wire by changing the magnetic field through it, by moving a magnet, moving the wire, or changing a current nearby. Generators and transformers work this way.
The voltage a source such as a battery, generator, or changing magnetic field produces to push charge around a circuit. Despite the name, it is a voltage, measured in volts, not a force.
A tiny, negatively charged particle found around every atom. In a metal wire, loosely held electrons drift along to carry electric current.
A sudden, often invisible flow of static electricity between objects that can silently destroy sensitive parts like MOSFETs and integrated circuits.
Rearranging the charges inside an object just by bringing a charged object near it, without touching. It is why a charged balloon can pull on a neutral wall or stream of water.
A dated record of a project's requirements, sketches, calculations, measurements, failures, and fixes, kept as you work so anyone can see how and why the design changed.
The unit of capacitance: one farad stores one coulomb of charge per volt. Real capacitors are usually measured in microfarads (µF), nanofarads (nF), or picofarads (pF).
A closed shell or mesh of conducting material whose free charges rearrange to cancel outside electric fields, so the space inside is shielded from static shocks and radio waves.
The rule that the voltage induced in a coil equals how fast the magnetic flux through it changes, times the number of turns. Faster change or more turns means more voltage.
The smooth, concave cone of solder that forms between a pad and a component lead in a well-wetted joint.
An input pin connected to nothing that holds it at a voltage, so it drifts with static and stray signals and reads random values; a pull-up or pull-down resistor fixes it.
A chemical cleaning agent, often built into the core of solder wire, that removes oxide from metal surfaces so molten solder can bond to them.
The roughly fixed voltage a diode or LED uses up when current flows through it the right way, about 2 V for a red LED and about 3 V for blue or white.
How many times something repeats each second, measured in hertz (Hz). 60 Hz AC completes 60 full back-and-forth cycles every second.

A safety part containing a thin metal link that melts and opens the circuit when current exceeds its rating. A multimeter's current inputs are protected by fuses; a blown fuse makes the meter read zero amps.
A machine that turns motion into electricity by spinning coils and magnets past each other, using electromagnetic induction.
A general-purpose input/output pin: a microcontroller pin your code can set as an input to read a signal or as an output to switch something on and off.
A logic circuit that adds two bits, producing a sum bit (XOR) and a carry bit (AND); chained full adders add whole binary numbers inside every processor.
A two-wire bus (SDA for data, SCL for clock) that lets one microcontroller talk to many sensors and displays, each with its own address.
A coil of wire that stores energy in a magnetic field and resists sudden changes in current.
A material, like plastic, rubber, or glass, whose electrons are held tightly, so current can barely flow through it.
A complete circuit of many transistors and other parts built onto one small chip of silicon, sealed in a package with pins. Pin 1 is marked by a dot or notch.
A circuit that turns direct current into alternating current, for example to run household devices from solar panels or a car battery. It is the opposite job of a rectifier.
At any junction in a circuit, the total current flowing in equals the total current flowing out; charge is never lost or piled up at a node.
Around any closed loop in a circuit, the voltage rises add up to the same total as the voltage drops, so the sum around the loop is zero.
A circuit of two gates whose outputs feed back into each other's inputs, so it holds a 0 or a 1 after the inputs return to rest: one bit of memory.
The rule that an induced current always flows in the direction that fights the change that made it. It is why a magnet falls slowly through a copper tube.
A diode that gives off light when current flows through it the right way. It is polarized: the longer leg (anode) goes toward +, and it needs a series resistor to limit its current.
The drop in a circuit's output voltage when something connected to it draws current, such as a load pulling a voltage divider's output below its calculated value.
A small circuit, built from transistors, that turns one or more HIGH/LOW inputs into a HIGH/LOW output following a rule such as NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR, or XOR.
The voltage ranges a digital circuit treats as 1 (HIGH) or 0 (LOW); on a 5 V Arduino, above about 3 V reads HIGH and below about 1.5 V reads LOW.
A circuit, often just a resistor and a capacitor, that lets slow changes through but smooths away fast ones such as noise or a bouncing button.
The invisible region around a magnet or a current-carrying wire where magnetic forces act. It is drawn as field lines from north to south.
How much magnetic field passes through a loop or coil: field strength times the area it crosses. Changing the flux is what induces a voltage.
A safety rating (CAT II, III, or IV, with a voltage) that tells where a meter can be used safely, based on how much energy a fault at that point in an electrical system could release.
A tiny computer on a single chip that reads inputs, runs one program over and over, and switches outputs. The brain of an Arduino.
One thousandth of an amp, written mA. Divide by 1000 to get amps before using Ohm's Law: 20 mA = 0.020 A.
A metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor: a transistor switched by voltage on its gate instead of current. Logic-level MOSFETs let an Arduino pin switch motors and LED strips.

A handheld instrument that measures several electrical quantities, usually voltage, current, and resistance, plus continuity and diode tests, by changing what it connects inside when you turn the dial.
A name attached to a schematic wire. Every wire with the same name is the same connection, even with no line drawn between them.
The unit of resistance, written Ω. One ohm lets one amp flow when one volt is applied. Named after Georg Simon Ohm.
A circuit with a gap in its path, such as an open switch, a broken wire, or a missing part, so no current can flow.
An instrument that draws a voltage as a moving graph over time, so you can see a signal’s shape, frequency, and amplitude instead of a single number.
The OL a meter shows when a measurement is too large for its range. In ohms or continuity mode it means there is no complete path between the probes: an open circuit.
A chemical reaction in which a metal surface combines with oxygen, leaving a dull or crusty layer that blocks a good electrical or solder connection.
A circuit with side-by-side branches, so every branch gets the full voltage and the current splits between them.
A resistor whose resistance drops as more light falls on it, from about a megohm in the dark to a few hundred ohms in bright light; paired with a fixed resistor it makes a light sensor.
Which side of a voltage is positive (+) and which is negative (−). DC keeps one polarity, AC keeps flipping it, and polarized parts like LEDs only work with their polarity the right way around.
An electronic part, like an LED, diode, or electrolytic capacitor, that only works when connected the right way around, with its + lead toward positive. Reversed, it does nothing or can be damaged.
A resistor with a third, sliding contact (the wiper) that you turn to choose any voltage between its two ends. Volume and brightness knobs are potentiometers.
A list of every part's current draw, added up to check that the power supply can deliver the peak current and to estimate how long a battery will last.
The most power a part can safely turn into heat, such as ¼ W for a common resistor. Stay well under it, about half, for a part that lasts.
A resistor that gently holds an input pin LOW until something connects it to the positive supply.
A resistor that gently holds an input pin HIGH until something, like a pressed button, connects it to ground. Without it the pin “floats” and reads random values.
Faking an in-between voltage by switching a pin fully on and off very fast. The longer each “on” pulse, the brighter an LED looks or the faster a motor spins.

Changing alternating current (AC) into direct current (DC) by letting current through in only one direction, usually with diodes. It is the first step inside almost every phone charger and power adapter.
A circuit, usually built from diodes, that changes alternating current into direct current. A bridge rectifier uses four diodes so both halves of the AC wave come out pointing the same way.
The letter-and-number name of a part on a schematic, like R1, C3, or U2. The same name appears on the circuit board and the parts list.
An electrically operated switch: a small current through a coil makes a magnet pull a separate set of contacts closed, so a low-power circuit can safely switch a high-power one.
A measure of how strongly a material opposes the flow of electric current, measured in ohms; a good solder joint keeps this as low as the wire itself.
A part that adds a set amount of resistance to a circuit, limiting current and dividing voltage. It is not polarized, and its value is shown by colored bands.
A solid resin, often derived from pine trees, used as the flux embedded in rosin-core solder to clean surfaces as they're heated.
A drawing of a circuit that uses standard symbols to show what connects to what, not where the parts physically sit.
A filled dot where wires meet on a schematic, showing that they are electrically joined. Crossing wires with no dot are not connected.
An input with two thresholds: it switches HIGH above the upper one and only switches back LOW below the lower one, so a slow or noisy signal produces one clean change.
A material such as silicon that conducts better than an insulator but worse than a metal, and whose conduction can be controlled. Diodes, LEDs, transistors, and chips are all made from it.
Sending data one bit at a time over a wire, the way an Arduino talks to a computer over USB through the Serial Monitor.
A circuit with only one path, so the same current flows through every part and the supply voltage is shared among them.
An unintended low-resistance path that lets current bypass the parts it should flow through. With almost no resistance, current rises sharply, heating wires and batteries and blowing fuses.
The smooth, repeating curve made by voltage from a spinning generator. Grid AC is a sine wave that rises, falls, and crosses zero twice each cycle.
Unwanted solder connecting two pads or pins that should be separate, creating a short circuit.
A coil of wire that becomes a magnet when current flows, often pulling a metal plunger in a straight line, as in door locks and valves.
Electric charge that builds up on a surface and stays put instead of flowing, until it jumps away as a spark or shock.
A marked spot in a circuit where you touch a meter probe to check that the voltage matches what the schematic predicts.
How much heat an object can soak up before its temperature rises. Thick wires and pads tied to large copper areas have high thermal mass and need more heat delivery to solder.
The gate voltage at which a MOSFET starts to conduct; a logic-level MOSFET is fully on well below 5 V, so an Arduino pin can drive it directly.
For a resistor and capacitor, τ = R × C, in seconds: the time to charge 63% of the way to the supply voltage (or discharge to 37%). After about five time constants the capacitor is essentially full.
Coating a soldering-iron tip or a wire end with a thin layer of fresh solder so heat transfers well and the surface resists oxidation.
Two coils wound around a shared iron core that use changing magnetism to raise or lower AC voltage. It only works with alternating current, which is a big reason the power grid uses AC.
A semiconductor switch or amplifier with three leads, where a small signal on one lead controls a much larger current through the other two. Billions of them make up every computer chip.
A table that lists every combination of a logic circuit's inputs and the output each combination produces.
The movement of fresh air through a space to carry away fumes, such as the flux smoke produced while soldering.
The electrical push between two points in a circuit, measured in volts (V). More voltage pushes more current through the same resistance.
Two resistors in series that split a voltage into a smaller one at the point between them, set by the ratio of the two resistances.
A part that holds its output at a steady voltage, such as 5 V or 3.3 V, even as the input voltage or the load current changes; use one, not a voltage divider, to power things.
The unit of power: how fast energy is used or turned into heat, light, or motion. One watt is one volt times one amp.
A graph of a signal over time, usually voltage up the side and time along the bottom, like the trace on an oscilloscope.
The way molten solder spreads smoothly across a clean, hot metal surface instead of beading up; good wetting is the sign of a sound joint.
